messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Vignette:
Marcus sits with a stillness that seems to cost him a great deal of effort, his hands clenched in his lap. At twenty-five, he works as a housekeeper for a large downtown hotel, a job he chose for its predictability and the fact that he can often work with headphones in, lost in his own world. This ability to drift away has become his primary coping mechanism, a way to escape a reality that feels perpetually unsafe. The memories of his childhood are not distant echoes but visceral, recurring events. He describes them as a film that plays without warning, not on a screen but inside his own body. When the memory of his father comes, it is always at night. He is a small child again in his bed, and the darkness in the room is absolute, a heavy, suffocating presence. He can feel the coarse, nubby texture of the old wool blanket being pressed down over him, scratching his cheek, and the smell of stale whiskey is so real he gags. He hears his own small cries, thin and reedy, and feels the familiar, terrifying surge of his father’s anger in response. When these moments hit, the hotel hallway he is cleaning vanishes, and he is back in that room, the overwhelming terror so potent that he has to brace himself against a wall, gasping for air until the world solidifies around him again.

These sensory fragments bleed into his daily life, turning mundane moments into sources of acute threat. Nighttime is the hardest; he sleeps with multiple lights on, a habit that began in adolescence and has only solidified. Waking up in the dark for any reason can trigger a full-blown panic attack, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape. The sound of a child crying, even a fussy baby in the hotel lobby or a toddler having a tantrum in the park, sends a jolt of ice through his veins. His body reacts before his mind can catch up: a cold sweat, tense muscles, and an immediate, overwhelming urge to flee. A few months ago, a guest left behind a wool throw blanket with a texture almost identical to the one from his childhood. Simply touching it to place it in the laundry cart caused him to recoil, his hand tingling as if burned. He stood frozen in the hotel room for ten minutes, his breath catching in his throat.

Over the years, Marcus has constructed a life designed to minimize these triggers. He is certain that his past is visible to others, that they can see the damage on him as if it were a physical scar. This belief makes him feel less like a person and more like an object to be scrutinized, and it fuels his deep-seated conviction that anyone, at any time, could hurt him. To manage this, he ensures he is never alone in a room with another person, especially men. He turns down invitations for coffee with coworkers and arranges to meet his few friends only in busy, public places. This has kept him single, as the prospect of intimacy is fused with the certainty of danger. At work, this fear had concrete consequences. He was recently offered a promotion to a supervisory role, a position that would have meant a significant pay raise, but he turned it down. The thought of conducting one-on-one staff meetings in a small office was unbearable, so he gave up the opportunity, retreating back into the relative safety of his cleaning cart and headphones.

He came to therapy after an incident at work last week. He was finishing a late shift when a child in an adjacent room began to cry inconsolably. The sound, echoing in the quiet, dark corridor, was the perfect storm. The memory replayed in full sensory detail, and he found himself crouching by his cart, shaking, fully convinced his father was about to appear at the end of the hall. A colleague found him, and the profound shame of being seen in that state was what finally broke through his avoidance. He is terrified of losing control completely, but beneath the fear is a fragile hope that he might one day be able to stand in a dark room or hear a child cry without his body screaming that he is about to die.
